title: Brain connectivity aberrations in anabolic-androgenic steroid users.
response:
This study, identified by PMID: 27942448, investigates the impact of anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) use on brain connectivity, focusing on its effects on impulsivity and related behaviors. The research utilized resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to analyze brain networks in a large cohort of 151 males engaged in heavy resistance strength training. Among these participants, 50 were confirmed AAS users based on urinary tests, while 16 were previous users and 59 served as non-users (controls).

The findings revealed reduced functional connectivity between key brain regions involved in emotional and cognitive regulation. Specifically, current AAS users showed decreased connectivity between the amygdala and the default-mode network (DMN), as well as between the dorsal attention network (DAN) and a frontal node that includes the superior and inferior frontal gyri (SFG/IFG) and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). These connectivity reductions were more pronounced with increased duration and frequency of AAS use.

These results suggest that AAS use may disrupt neural networks critical for emotional and cognitive control, potentially contributing to the observed behavioral consequences such as aggression and impulsivity. title: Role of White Matter Microstructure in Impulsive Behavior.
response:
This study explores the relationship between white matter microstructure and impulsivity in a group of healthy adults. The researchers used diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to assess white matter integrity and the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale-11 to evaluate impulsivity, which includes subdomains of attentional, motor, and nonplanning impulsiveness.

The findings indicate that lower fractional anisotropy (FA), a measure of white matter microstructure, is associated with higher levels of motor impulsiveness, suggesting that reduced white matter integrity in certain tracts might contribute to increased impulsivity. Specifically, the corticospinal tract showed a significant inverse correlation with motor impulsiveness. Additionally, higher FA was found to be associated with greater nonplanning impulsiveness, as indicated by a positive correlation with regional FA values in the superior fronto-occipital fasciculus.

These results support the hypothesis that impulsivity, particularly its motor and nonplanning components, can be linked to specific white matter microstructural connectivity patterns. This study provides initial evidence that impulsivity is partly a network-based construct, involving white matter microstructural integrity even in healthy populations. title: Behavioral and cognitive impulsivity in obsessive-compulsive disorder and eating disorders.
response:

The research utilized both self-report measures and neurocognitive tasks to assess impulsivity and response inhibition.

Participants completed the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11) for self-reported impulsivity and a stop-signal reaction time task to measure response inhibition. Additionally, they were evaluated for OCD and ED symptoms using the Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale and Eating Disorders Examination-Questionnaire.

The findings indicated that both OCD and ED patients reported higher levels of impulsivity compared to healthy controls, as measured by the BIS-11. However, only the OCD group showed increased stop-signal reaction times, suggesting a specific impairment in inhibitory control. The authors propose that heightened self-reported impulsivity in OCD and ED might be linked to anxiety experienced by these patient groups, while the lack of inhibitory control observed in OCD could indicate a distinct behavioral deficit.

title: Head Motion and Inattention/Hyperactivity Share Common Genetic Influences: Implications for fMRI Studies of ADHD.
response:
This study explores the relationship between head motion (HM) during functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans and inattention/hyperactivity-impulsivity (ADHD symptoms) in a sample of healthy young adult twins. The research indicates that there is a moderate genetic overlap between HM and ADHD symptoms, specifically in terms of inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity. The genetic correlation between HM and inattention was found to be 0.24 (95% CI: 0.02, 0.43), while the correlation with hyperactivity-impulsivity was 0.23 (95% CI: 0.07, 0.39).

The findings suggest that treating HM as a nuisance covariate in neuroimaging studies of ADHD may reduce the ability to detect true group differences because HM and ADHD symptoms share common genetic influences. This implies that the assumption of independence between HM and ADHD symptoms is not valid, which can lead to an increased risk of false positives in fMRI studies of ADHD.

title: Investigation of structure-function correlation among the young offspring of patients with bipolar disorder.

The research involved 16 participants aged between 12 and 18 years old. The participants underwent both clinical assessments and neurocognitive testing, along with structural brain MRI and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI).

title: Insula Connectivity Abnormalities Predict Impulsivity in Chronic Heroin Use Disorder: A Cross-Sectional Resting-State fMRI Study.
response:
This study, identified by PMID: 38002468, investigates the relationship between impulsivity and neural connectivity in individuals with chronic heroin use disorder (HUD). The research employs a cross-sectional design using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) and the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11) to assess trait impulsivity, which is categorized into three components: motor, attentional, and nonplanning impulsivity.

The findings indicate that individuals with HUD exhibit higher levels of total trait impulsivity, motor impulsivity, and nonplanning impulsivity compared to healthy controls. Specifically, the study identifies significant correlations between trait impulsivity and functional connectivity (FC) patterns involving the insula. Notably, increased FC between the right insula and the lateral occipital cortex and the right angular gyrus was positively associated with total trait impulsivity scores, motor impulsivity, and nonplanning impulsivity. Conversely, decreased FC between the left insula and the left superior frontal gyrus and left frontopolar brain regions was negatively associated with trait impulsivity.

title: Functional connectivity of emotional well-being: Overconnectivity between default and attentional networks is associated with attitudes of anger and aggression.
response:
This study, identified by PMID: 31401546, explores the relationship between functional connectivity in the brain and emotional well-being, specifically focusing on attitudes of anger and aggression. Using data from the Human Connectome Project, the researchers employed two methods to assess functional connectivity. The first method involved principal component analysis of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, which revealed that typicality scores of functional connectivity were significantly correlated with emotional health metrics related to anger and aggression in three out of ten principal components. 

The second method examined functional connectivity between pairs of resting-state networks, finding a positive correlation between the default and attentional networks and scores of anger and aggression. This suggests that overconnectivity between these networks may be associated with increased impulsivity and difficulty in managing emotions, particularly anger and aggression. The findings support the hypothesis that impaired effortful control and decreased response inhibition could be mechanisms underlying these emotional attitudes, potentially linking them to broader issues of impulsivity.

title: Neural Basis of Increased Cognitive Control of Impulsivity During the Mid-Luteal Phase Relative to the Late Follicular Phase of the Menstrual Cycle.
response:

The research compares event-related monetary delay discounting task behavior and concurrent fMRI brain activity between women in the mid-luteal phase (LP) and those in the late follicular phase (FP).

The findings indicate that women in the late follicular phase exhibit greater responsiveness to short-term rewards, as evidenced by a higher discount rate, and show increased activity in the dorsal striatum (DS). This increased activity in the DS correlates with functional connectivity between the DS and the dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), suggesting that the DS-dlPFC circuitry plays a regulatory role in impulsivity. Additionally, the right dlPFC is more active in the mid-luteal phase compared to the late follicular phase, and this effect is sensitive to estradiol levels. The study also finds that DS-dlPFC functional connectivity magnitude correlates negatively with psychometric impulsivity scores during the late follicular phase, indicating that relative estradiol levels may enhance cognitive control over impulsivity.

title: Human Brain Imaging Links Dopaminergic Systems to Impulsivity.
response:

The research highlights that both molecular and functional imaging methods, particularly when combined with pharmacological probes, provide strong evidence linking striatal dopaminergic function to various aspects of impulsivity. Specifically, the study indicates that striatal D2-type dopamine receptors (D2 and D3) play a crucial role in cognitive control and reward-based decision-making processes.

The findings suggest that lower levels of D2-type receptor availability in the striatum are associated with higher self-reported impulsivity and poorer motor response inhibition and cognitive flexibility. Additionally, impulsive choices in reward-based decision-making tasks are linked to deficits in striatal D2-type dopamine receptor availability, with evidence pointing to an inverted U-shaped relationship where optimal performance is achieved at a moderate level of striatal dopaminergic activity.

The study further supports these findings by examining both clinical populations with striatal dopamine D2-type receptor deficits and healthy control groups, indicating that targeting D2-type receptors could be beneficial for improving cognitive control. title: Dorsal striatal functional connectivity changes in Internet gaming disorder: A longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging study.
response:

The participants were re-evaluated approximately one year later, allowing for the examination of both structural and functional brain changes associated with IGD.

title: [A review of functional electrical stimulation based on brain-computer interface].
response:
The abstract discusses the application of functional electrical stimulation (FES) based on brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) for individuals with motor dysfunction due to central nervous system damage. This method aims to bridge the gap between neural signals and muscle contractions, thereby promoting nerve function recovery. The review covers three main areas: BCI paradigms, FES parameters, and rehabilitation efficacy. 

In terms of BCI paradigms, the review highlights various methods used to interpret neural signals, which are crucial for initiating FES. FES parameters, such as the timing and intensity of electrical impulses, are also discussed, emphasizing their importance in achieving effective muscle contractions and limb movements. The efficacy of this approach in rehabilitation is noted, particularly for conditions like stroke and spinal cord injury, where traditional rehabilitation methods may be less effective due to long treatment cycles and high costs.

While the abstract does not directly address impulsivity, it indirectly touches upon the neural mechanisms involved in motor control, which can be related to impulsivity in certain contexts. Impulsivity often involves difficulties in controlling actions and behaviors, which could be improved through better motor control facilitated by FES and BCIs. Future developments in this technology are anticipated to enhance its effectiveness and accessibility, potentially leading to more comprehensive treatments for neurological disorders.

title: Emotion dysregulation, impulsivity and anger rumination in borderline personality disorder: the role of amygdala and insula.
response:

The study included 28 BPD patients and 28 matched healthy controls who underwent brain MRI scans and neuropsychiatric assessments. Key findings include:

1. **Amygdala Volume**: Female BPD patients exhibited reduced right amygdala volumes, which correlated with measures of emotion regulation difficulties, depression, and rumination. This suggests that amygdala volume reductions may be particularly relevant for understanding emotional and behavioral dysregulation in women with BPD.

2. **Insula Cortical Thickness**: BPD patients showed a lower left insula cortical thickness, which negatively correlated with the Anger Rumination Scale. This indicates that structural changes in the insula might contribute to the tendency to ruminate over feelings of anger.

title: Testing the triple network model of psychopathology in a transdiagnostic neurodevelopmental cohort.
response:
This study investigates the triple network model of psychopathology, which suggests that altered connectivity between the Salience Network (SN), Central Executive Network (CEN), and Default Mode Network (DMN) may underlie neurodevelopmental conditions. The research was conducted on a transdiagnostic cohort of 175 children (60 girls) experiencing neurodevelopmental difficulties, including hyperactivity/impulsivity and inattention, as well as a comparison group of 60 children (33 girls).

Using resting-state functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data, the researchers found that hyperactivity/impulsivity was associated with increased functional connectivity between the SN, CEN, and DMN in the at-risk children. Conversely, in the comparison group, hyperactivity/impulsivity was linked to decreased functional connectivity between the CEN and DMN. These findings were consistent across different adult parcellations of brain function and even when applying more stringent criteria for motion during the imaging process.

The results indicate that altered connectivity within these networks may characterize transdiagnostic neurodevelopmental difficulties, particularly hyperactivity/impulsivity. title: Hippocampus Functional Connectivity, Impulsivity, and Subsequent Substance Use.
response:
This study, identified by PMID:40297839, explores the relationship between impulsivity and subsequent substance use (specifically tobacco and marijuana) in adolescents through the lens of hippocampal functional connectivity (rsFC). The research utilized data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, focusing on resting-state fMRI scans to assess the connectivity of the hippocampus with several key brain networks, including the cingulo-parietal network, visual network, sensory-motor network, and default mode network (DMN).

The study found that baseline hippocampal rsFC with these networks had marginal associations with future substance use. More importantly, it demonstrated that hippocampal rsFC was significantly related to impulsivity, which then predicted higher levels of substance use at follow-up. This suggests that hippocampal connectivity may mediate the link between impulsivity and substance use behaviors in adolescents.

The findings highlight the potential role of hippocampal functional connectivity in understanding the neural mechanisms underlying risk behaviors such as substance use. This research underscores the importance of considering brain connectivity when developing interventions aimed at reducing substance use among adolescents.

title: Brain functional connectivity changes in children that differ in impulsivity temperamental trait.
response:
This study, published in 2014 in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience (PMID: 24834038), explores the relationship between impulsivity and brain functional connectivity in typically developing children. Using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure brain functional connectivity at rest and impulsivity scores derived from parent-reported questionnaires, the researchers identified specific areas within the default mode network (DMN) that showed negative correlations with impulsivity scores. Specifically, they found that the posterior cingulate cortex and the right angular gyrus had reduced functional connectivity with other regions in high-impulsive children compared to their low-impulsive counterparts.

The study also observed that the typical anti-phasic relationship between the DMN and the action-related network was diminished in children with higher levels of impulsivity. This suggests that impulsivity may influence the way different brain networks interact during rest, potentially reflecting underlying differences in cognitive and emotional processing.

Overall, this research provides novel insights into how individual differences in personality traits can shape brain function in a developmentally typical population, bridging the gap between psychological assessments and neuroimaging techniques.

title: Brain Networks Associated With COVID-19 Risk: Data From 3662 Participants.
response:

2. Increased internal connectivity was noted within the default mode, ventral salience, subcortical, and sensorimotor networks.
3. Enhanced connectivity was observed between the ventral salience, subcortical, and sensorimotor networks.

title: Go/No-Go task performance predicts differences in compulsivity but not in impulsivity personality traits.
response:
This study, published in 2017 in Psychiatry Research (PMID: 28783574), investigated the relationship between performance on the Go/No-Go task and personality traits related to impulsivity and compulsivity. The Go/No-Go task is used to measure inhibitory control, specifically the ability to withhold inappropriate responses. The researchers divided 63 healthy participants into two groups based on their false alarm rates during the task. They then assessed these participants using the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11) and the Maudsley Obsessional Compulsive Questionnaire (MOCI).

The findings indicated that participants with higher false alarm rates (H-FA) exhibited a higher risk-taking strategy and scored higher on the MOCI Total and MOCI Checking subscales, which are associated with compulsive behaviors. Importantly, there was no significant correlation between Go/No-Go task performance and scores on the BIS-11, which measures various aspects of impulsivity. title: Exploring variability in basal ganglia connectivity with functional MRI in healthy aging.
response:
This study, identified by PMID: 29442271, investigates the functional connectivity (FC) within the basal ganglia network (BGN) in healthy older adults, focusing on its relationship with dopaminergic processes and other factors such as impulsive behavior. Using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from 486 participants in the Whitehall-II imaging sub-study, the researchers employed both region-of-interest (ROI) and voxel-based approaches to analyze FC patterns. 

The findings indicate that age is the primary factor significantly associated with changes in FC within the BGN, suggesting that alterations in the dopaminergic system might contribute to these changes. However, the study did not find any specific dopamine-related functions that could explain the observed FC variations beyond what is already evident in healthy aging. Notably, the study did not identify a unique link between FC in the BGN and impulsive behavior, indicating that while age-related changes in the BGN are influenced by dopaminergic processes, impulsive behavior does not appear to play a distinct role in modulating these connections in healthy aging individuals.

title: Functional connectivity in resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) in opioid use disorder.
response:

Special Topics* (PMID: 41098388), explores the functional connectivity in resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) among individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD). The study highlights how opioid addiction affects key brain networks, particularly the default mode network (DMN), salience network (SN), and executive control network (ECN).

The review begins by discussing the neurological basis of opioid addiction and the principles of rs-fMRI, along with the various methodologies used in such research. It also addresses the inconsistencies and methodological challenges that can complicate the interpretation of findings. The authors then present their own research, which involved 42 participants—23 healthy controls and 19 patients with OUD. Each participant underwent MRI scans including structural, resting-state, and task sequences, with data processed using the CONN Toolbox in MATLAB.

Key findings indicate significant disruptions in functional connectivity within the DMN and SN networks in individuals with OUD. title: Neural processes during response inhibition in complex posttraumatic stress disorder.
response:
This study, identified by PMID: 34964209, investigates the neural mechanisms underlying impulsivity in individuals with Complex Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (CPTSD). The research employed a Go/NoGo response inhibition task using both functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electroencephalogram (EEG) to examine neural activity in CPTSD patients (n=30), PTSD patients (n=40), and healthy controls (n=40).

Key findings indicate reduced bilateral thalamic activation in CPTSD patients compared to both PTSD patients and healthy controls during inhibition tasks. Notably, there were no significant differences in functional connectivity between the thalamus and other cognitive control regions among the three groups. Additionally, no group differences were observed in EEG responses.

These results suggest that CPTSD is characterized by distinct neural processes in inhibitory control, particularly involving the thalamus, which may contribute to the impulsivity often observed in this condition. This finding highlights the importance of the thalamus in understanding the neural underpinnings of response inhibition in CPTSD and differentiates it from PTSD, where no such differences were found.

title: Response inhibition and impulsivity: an fMRI study.
response:

title: What is attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder?
response: The abstract from the 1999 article by Swanson et al. (PMID: 10570690) highlights the core symptoms of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), which include significant impairments in sustained attention and impulsivity, alongside overactivity. Impulsivity is a critical aspect of ADHD, often manifesting as difficulty in controlling actions and emotions. Neuroimaging studies have suggested that individuals with ADHD might exhibit differences in the circuitry involving frontal cortical-basal ganglia connections, though the specificity and robustness of these findings are still under investigation. While the abstract does not provide extensive details on neuroimaging techniques used, it underscores the importance of understanding the neural basis of ADHD, particularly in relation to impulsivity. The authors also note that ADHD symptoms are heritable but highlight the need for further research into the exact etiological factors and optimal treatment strategies.

title: Enhanced ADHD classification through deep learning and dynamic resting state fMRI analysis.
response:
This study, identified by the PMID 39424632, explores the use of deep learning techniques to enhance the classification of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) using dynamic resting-state functional connectivity (rs-fMRI) analysis. The research employs a novel deep learning network called Skip-Vote-Net, which leverages dynamic connectivity patterns derived from rs-fMRI data. The study involved 222 participants from the NYU dataset within the ADHD-200 database, including both ADHD and typically developing children (TDC).

The methodology involves constructing functional connectivity matrices from overlapping segments using Pearson's correlation between mean time series of 116 regions of interest defined by the AAL 116 atlas. Skip-Vote-Net uses a majority voting mechanism to classify ADHD from TDC and further distinguishes between the inattentive subtype (ADHDI) and the predominantly combined subtype (ADHDC).

title: Binge drinking is associated with altered resting state functional connectivity of reward-salience and top down control networks.
response: This study, identified by PMID: 31073695, explores the neural correlates of binge drinking using resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) analysis in young adults. The research focuses on the altered connectivity within key brain networks involved in reward processing, salience detection, and top-down control. Specifically, the study found that binge drinkers (BDs) showed increased connectivity between the striatal reward regions (nucleus accumbens and caudate nucleus) and the orbitofrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), which is consistent with previous findings in alcohol use disorders (AUDs). This enhanced connectivity might reflect alcohol-motivated appetitive behaviors. In contrast, BDs exhibited reduced connectivity between the inferior frontal cortex (IFC) and the hippocampus, which correlated with higher levels of craving. This reduced connectivity suggests difficulties in inhibitory control and the inability to recall the negative consequences of heavy drinking, potentially contributing to the continuation of binge drinking behaviors. The findings highlight the importance of network-level dysregulation in the development and maintenance of binge drinking patterns, providing insights into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying this form of alcohol consumption.

title: Cortical folding patterns are associated with impulsivity in healthy young adults.
response: This study, published in 2017 in the journal *Brain Imaging and Behavior* (PMID: 27743376), explores the relationship between impulsivity and cortical folding in healthy young adults. The researchers utilized magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure the local gyrification index (LGI) and assessed impulsivity using the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11). They found that impulsivity, particularly in its attention, motor, and non-planning subdomains, was positively correlated with cortical folding in various brain regions, including the postcentral gyrus, cingulate gyrus, precentral gyrus, inferior frontal gyrus, middle temporal gyrus, superior parietal gyrus, and occipital gyrus. These findings suggest that alterations in early brain development, as indicated by cortical folding, may contribute to higher levels of impulsivity in healthy individuals. Additionally, the study revealed gender-specific differences in the correlation between BIS-11 scores and LGI in certain frontal gyri, highlighting the importance of considering sex when studying these relationships. Overall, this research underscores the potential of cortical folding as a marker of early brain development and its relevance to understanding impulsivity in young adults.

title: Prefrontal Cortical Connectivity Mediates Locus Coeruleus Noradrenergic Regulation of Inhibitory Control in Older Adults.
response:

2. **Prefrontal Connectivity**: Stronger connectivity between the presupplementary motor area (preSMA) and the right inferior frontal gyrus (rIFG) was observed in individuals with better response inhibition. However, no significant correlation was found with the volumes of prefrontal cortical regions.

title: Resting-state brain networks alterations in adolescents with Internet Gaming Disorder associate with cognitive control impairments.
response:
This study, as reported in the article with PMID 39315326, investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive control impairments in adolescents with Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD). The researchers used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to analyze resting-state brain networks in a sample of 44 adolescents diagnosed with IGD and 50 healthy controls. Key findings include:

title: Nature of functional links in valuation networks differentiates impulsive behaviors between abstinent heroin-dependent subjects and nondrug-using subjects.
response:
This study, identified by the PMID 25944613, explores the neural mechanisms underlying impulsivity in abstinent heroin-dependent individuals compared to non-drug users using resting-state functional MRI. The research highlights the importance of functional connectivity within specific brain networks—namely, the δ-network (involved in executive control) and the β-network (part of the reward system). 

The study found that in non-drug users, there is a balanced functional connection between these two networks, with the δ-network exerting competitive control over impulsivity. Conversely, in abstinent heroin-dependent subjects, this balance is disrupted, showing increased connectivity in the β-network and decreased connectivity in the δ-network. This imbalance is correlated with higher levels of impulsivity. The authors suggest that this imbalance may reflect a mutual reinforcement between the reward and executive control systems, which could contribute to the behavioral abnormalities observed in individuals recovering from heroin addiction.

These findings provide insights into the neural basis of impulsivity in addiction and propose that the altered functional connectivity between the β- and δ-networks might serve as a biomarker for assessing self-control capacity in individuals with a history of substance abuse.

title: Functional connectivity alterations in individuals with gaming disorder assessed by functional magnetic resonance imaging: a systematic review.
response:

title: Trait impulsivity components correlate differently with proactive and reactive control.
response:
This study explores the relationship between trait impulsivity and cognitive control mechanisms using neuroimaging techniques. The researchers used the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale to measure three components of impulsivity—motor, attention, and non-planning—and assessed cognitive control through a hybrid Stroop task that differentiates between proactive and reactive control processes. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was employed to observe brain activity during the task.

The findings indicate that different aspects of impulsivity are associated with distinct cognitive control networks. Specifically, higher levels of motor impulsiveness were linked to enhanced proactive control in the inferior parietal lobule but reduced reactive control in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and anterior cingulate cortex. Similarly, greater attention impulsiveness correlated with diminished proactive control in the right DLPFC. These results suggest that the various components of impulsivity may target different cognitive control subsystems, highlighting the complexity of the relationship between impulsivity traits and neural mechanisms underlying cognitive control.

title: Youth Screen Media Activity Patterns and Associations With Behavioral Developmental Measures and Resting-state Brain Functional Connectivity.
response:

The study found that the video-centric higher-frequency SMA pattern persisted over time, with 30.4% of participants still exhibiting this pattern one year later. The study highlights the importance of considering specific types of SMA rather than overall screen time when examining its effects on youth development.

title: Neural correlates of aggression in personality disorders from the perspective of DSM-5 maladaptive traits: a systematic review.

title: Decisional impulsivity and the associative-limbic subthalamic nucleus in obsessive-compulsive disorder: stimulation and connectivity.
response: This study explores the relationship between decisional impulsivity and the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) who have undergone deep brain stimulation (DBS). These findings have significant clinical implications, particularly for the behavioral and cognitive effects of STN stimulation in psychiatric disorders and the neuropsychiatric symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

title: Altered resting-state frontoparietal control network in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.

title: Delay discounting is associated with the fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations and resting-state functional connectivity in late adolescence.
response: This study explores the relationship between delay discounting (DD), a measure of impulsivity, and neuroimaging metrics in late adolescents. title: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging alterations in borderline personality disorder: A systematic review.
response:
This systematic review, based on 15 rs-fMRI studies, highlights significant alterations in resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) in individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD). The review, published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, emphasizes that these alterations are observed within and between key brain networks, such as the Default Mode Network (DMN), Salience Network (SN), and Central Executive Network (CEN).

Key findings include aberrant rs-FC within these networks and between them, as well as specific functional impairments in regions like the bilateral amygdala, anterior and posterior cingulate cortex, hippocampus, and prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that BPD is associated with disrupted communication between different brain regions, particularly those involved in emotional regulation and cognitive control.

However, the review also notes several limitations, including the observational nature of the studies, small sample sizes, the predominance of female participants, high rates of comorbid conditions, and variations in imaging methodologies. Despite these limitations, the study provides valuable insights into the neural underpinnings of BPD, particularly regarding impulsivity and emotion dysregulation.

Future research should employ multimodal approaches and longitudinal designs to better understand the neural correlates of BPD and potentially inform treatment strategies.

title: Neural connectivity moderates the association between sleep and impulsivity in adolescents.

response:

Utilizing a retrospective analysis of 56 PD patients who underwent bilateral STN-DBS, the researchers employed principal component analysis (PCA) to compress extensive neuropsychiatric and neuropsychological outcome scores into four main dimensions. These dimensions were interpreted to represent general non-motor improvement, mood and cognition improvement with trait impulsivity worsening, cognition improvement alone, and empathy and impulsive-compulsive behavior improvement.

The study identified specific structural connections between the frontal cortex and the subthalamic nucleus that were associated with changes along these dimensions. By stimulating these tracts, the researchers were able to estimate changes in individual symptom outcomes. In an independent validation dataset of 68 patients, the tract model successfully predicted changes in depression outcomes.

The findings suggest that specific neural pathways may be targeted to modulate particular non-motor symptoms, including impulsivity, through STN-DBS. title: Resting-state beta and gamma activity in Internet addiction.
response:

Key findings indicated that individuals with Internet addiction exhibited higher impulsivity and impaired inhibitory control compared to the control group. Neuroimaging results revealed that the Internet addiction group had lower absolute power in the beta band and higher absolute power in the gamma band during resting-state EEG recordings. response:

title: A multi-dimensional evaluation of craving and impulsivity among people admitted for alcohol-related problems in emergency department.
response:
